Project 01 · Mechanical design & fabrication

Mini Portable Pothole Filler

BTech final-year project · Vidya Academy of Science & Technology · 2019–2020 · group of four · AutoCAD and Fusion 360

The brief

Conventional pothole repair in India relies on large asphalt plants and crews, which is slow and expensive for small potholes and cracks. The brief was a compact unit that heats bitumen, mixes it with aggregate and compacts the patch in one pass, operated by one or two people.

My contribution

  • Mechanical design and 2D/3D drawings of the assemblies
  • Component selection and motor sizing for the mixer and rammer drives
  • Material selection across mild steel, cast iron and aluminium alloy
  • Cost estimation for the full build, around ₹19,500
  • Fabrication and testing of a reduced-scale working prototype

Design summary

  • Mixer: 310 mm mild steel dome, belt-driven by a 250 W / 24 V / 360 rpm DC gear motor, tilted through a cast iron gear and handwheel to discharge
  • Furnace: cast iron tar can (240 × 250 × 260 mm) hinged to the frame, gas burner and cylinder, tilting to pour molten bitumen into the mixer
  • Rammer: 390 mm mild steel bar with 63 mm head, driven by a 500 W / 24 V / 2500 rpm motor through a crankshaft and connecting rod, supported on ball bearings
  • Base: 1500 × 900 mm welded frame with 360° castors, wheel locks, control box and push handles

Outcome

A reduced-scale prototype was fabricated and tested, demonstrating the heat–mix–compact sequence in a single portable unit. Further work identified: scaling to the full design dimensions and adding automated pothole sensing.

Project 02 · System modelling & simulation

Demountable Fuel Cell Range Extender for Battery Electric Cars

MSc Energy Engineering dissertation · De Montfort University · 2023 · supervisor Dr Rupert Gammon · awarded with Distinction

The problem

Battery electric cars are limited on long journeys by range and charging time. Fuel cell range extenders are normally built into the vehicle, which requires design changes and carries the extra mass permanently, reducing efficiency on every journey.

The concept

A demountable range extender towed behind the car and connected through the existing external charging port. It is attached only when extra range is needed, so the vehicle needs no modification and carries no permanent weight penalty.

Method

  • Two MATLAB/Simulink vehicle models simulated over the WLTP Class 3 drive cycle (23.266 km per run)
  • Baseline: 1500 kg vehicle, 160 kW DC motor at 100 V, 62 kWh lithium-ion pack at 400 V nominal and 155 Ah, driven through a longitudinal driver block and H-bridge
  • With extender: 1750 kg including a 250 kg trailer carrying a 50 kW, 625 V DC proton exchange membrane fuel cell, battery starting at 20% state of charge
  • Outputs analysed: distance, state of charge, battery current and voltage, and speed against drive cycle demand

Findings

  • Charging from 20% to 100% while driving took about one hour, covering 36.76 km on the move with no stop at a charging station
  • Single-journey range rose from 170 km to approximately 376 km, with the battery full again at the end of that run
  • The 250 kg mass penalty applies only when the extender is fitted, unlike a built-in range extender
  • Further work: energy efficiency analysis, prototype development, real-world testing, cost analysis and hydrogen supply infrastructure
